gap: No result ChatGPT got states that a conventional direct-on-line well-pump motor draws up to seven times its nominal current in the first milliseconds of starting, while a soft-start pump or drive ramps to full speed over about 2 seconds. That inrush is what decides whether an inverter's surge rating can start the pump at all.
standout_why: Compared against the cited Franklin SubDrive/MonoDrive FAQ, the cited SubDrive Connect product page and the uncited top Franklin results. The FAQ only says soft start gives 'lower start-up current compared to conventional water systems' and 'Two-wire motors do not have soft start ability'. The SubDrive Connect page says 'Soft start maximizes system life' and gives no starting-current figure. Neither page states how large the inrush is or mentions inverters or generators at all. ChatGPT's own answer said only 'high surge capacity' and gave no number.
decides: This turns 'high surge' into a number you can check. A Franklin 1 HP 230 V 2-wire motor is rated 8.2 A full load and 10.4 A at service factor. At up to 7× that is roughly 13–17 kVA for the first instant. That is an inference: it applies Grundfos's generic multiple to a Franklin motor, because Franklin's locked-rotor table could not be read. On that figure, the 18,000 W low-frequency split-phase units (Sun Gold Power 6000W 48V, AIMS 6000W) clear it. The Victron MultiPlus-II's 9,000 VA peak and the EG4 6000XP's 12,000 W surge fall below it for a 1 HP direct-on-line motor. They become plausible only for smaller motors, or when the pump soft-starts (Grundfos SQ/SQE, or a Franklin SubDrive on a 3-wire or 3-phase motor). It confirms the page's current pick of a low-frequency 18 kW-surge split-phase unit for 1 HP-class 240 V pumps. It also adds a second route: a soft-start pump lets a smaller inverter work.
candidates: Sun Gold Power SPH6548P 6.5 kW hybrid

findings.label: Starting current of a conventional direct-on-line (DOL) 4-inch well-pump motor
findings.value: up to 7× nominal current in the first milliseconds
findings.source_title: SQ/SQE Protection features: Soft Start (Grundfos eCademy)
findings.note: Grundfos calls DOL 'the most common starting method for 4" conventional pumps' and says motor current can be 'up to seven times higher than the nominal value' during the first milliseconds.

findings.label: Soft-start time to reach nominal speed
findings.source_title: SQ/SQE Protection features: Soft Start (Grundfos eCademy)
findings.note: The SQ/SQE motor 'reaches the nominal value within a period of 2 seconds'. This avoids the DOL inrush, so a smaller inverter can start it.

findings.label: Soft start limitation
findings.value: Soft start gives lower start-up current; two-wire motors have no soft start
findings.note: Cited rival page. It says the drive 'starts and increases the motor speed slowly' with 'lower start-up current compared to conventional water systems', and that 'Two-wire motors do not have soft start ability.' It gives no figure. Input must be 190–260 VAC (F2 fault below 180 VAC), so the drive needs a 240 V inverter.

findings.label: Full-load / service-factor current
findings.value: 8.2 A full load, 10.4 A service factor, 230 VAC
findings.note: Arithmetic: 8.2 A × 230 V = 1,886 VA; × 7 = 13.2 kVA. 10.4 A × 230 V = 2,392 VA; × 7 = 16.7 kVA. This is an upper-bound estimate using Grundfos's generic 'up to 7×' figure, not Franklin's published locked-rotor amps, which this page does not list.
